facts.text: Mr. T as B.A. Baracus on The A-Team became one of the most recognizable TV characters of the 1980s
Despite constant gunfire and explosions, no one was ever killed in The A-Team
Mr. T was cast in The A-Team after Sylvester Stallone spotted him in a televised tough-man competition
George Peppard, who played Hannibal, reportedly didn't get along well with Mr. T on set throughout the series

David Hasselhoff's contract for Knight Rider gave him final approval over storylines involving his character

Cheers was filmed entirely at Paramount Studios in Hollywood
The Cheers theme song 'Where Everybody Knows Your Name' was written by Gary Portnoy and Judy Hart Angelo
Cheers debuted in 1982 with very low ratings and nearly got cancelled after its first season before building

Meredith Baxter and Michael Gross, who played the Keaton parents on Family Ties, were so convincing that fans often thought they were married

Diff'rent Strokes was one of the first American sitcoms to feature a primarily Black cast adopted into a wealthy
The Cosby Show is credited with reviving the sitcom format in the mid-1980s after the genre had fallen out

The Huxtables' home on The Cosby Show was set in a Brooklyn brownstone, giving the show a grounded urban setting
Leonardo DiCaprio joined Growing Pains in its sixth season and was so outstanding that he attracted attention

Kirk Cameron, star of Growing Pains, became a born-again Christian during the show's run

ALF stood for Alien Life Form — the character's actual name on his home planet Melmac was Gordon Shumway

Richard Dean Anderson, who played MacGyver, was a hockey player before turning to acting
MacGyver famously never carried a gun, a character choice that made the show stand out from other action series

Airwolf's helicopter was a real Bell 222 modified with fake weapons pods and aerodynamic add-ons for the show
The Airwolf helicopter was later sold to a German air ambulance service after the show ended
Jan-Michael Vincent, who starred in Airwolf, was reportedly one of the highest-paid TV actors of the early 1980s
The Dukes of Hazzard went through 309 General Lee Dodge Chargers during its run
The General Lee's horn played the first 12 notes of 'Dixie,' which became inseparable from the show's identity
John Schneider lied about his age to get cast in The Dukes of Hazzard — he said he was 24 when he was actually 18
Simon & Simon ran for eight seasons on CBS and became one of the highest-rated detective dramas of the early 1980s
Simon & Simon featured two brothers with opposite personalities as private detectives
The 'Who shot J.R.?' cliffhanger from Dallas in 1980 remains one of the most watched single episodes in American
The answer to 'Who shot J.R.?' in Dallas was kept secret from almost the entire cast and crew until the episode aired
Dallas spawned numerous international adaptations and is credited with popularizing the nighttime soap opera
Dynasty was created specifically to compete with Dallas and quickly surpassed it in the ratings by the mid-1980s
Joan Collins was cast in Dynasty after the producers saw her in a TV movie and decided to rewrite the show
Dynasty's Alexis Carrington, played by Joan Collins, became one of the most iconic TV villains of the 1980s
The Facts of Life spun off from Diff'rent Strokes, following Mrs. Garrett as housemother at an all-girls school
The Facts of Life started with a large ensemble cast that was trimmed to four main girls after the first season
Saved by the Bell evolved from a Saturday morning show called Good Morning, Miss Bliss
Mark-Paul Gosselaar, who played Zack Morris on Saved by the Bell, later built a successful dramatic TV career
Dustin Diamond, who played Screech on Saved by the Bell, faced serious legal troubles as an adult including a 2015 stabbing conviction

Patrick Stewart was initially reluctant to shave his head for Captain Picard

Whoopi Goldberg lobbied to appear on Star Trek: TNG because she credited the original series' Uhura with inspiring her as a young Black actress

Ed O'Neill, who played Al Bundy, had a brief tryout with the Pittsburgh Steelers before becoming an actor

Joe Cocker's 'With a Little Help from My Friends' became iconic as The Wonder Years' theme song

Roseanne broke ground showing a working-class American family when most sitcoms featured affluent characters
The fictional Conner family in Roseanne lived in Lanford, Illinois
Full House debuted in 1987 and was originally expected to be cancelled quickly
The Olsen twins, Mary-Kate and Ashley, shared the role of Michelle Tanner in Full House because of child labor

Scott Bakula performed many of his own stunts on Quantum Leap
The Quantum Leap finale remains one of the most controversial series endings
Moonlighting is credited with helping launch Bruce Willis's career
Moonlighting regularly broke the fourth wall and used experimental formats

Edward Woodward played Robert McCall in The Equalizer
The Equalizer's New York City setting was filmed almost entirely on location, giving it a grittier atmosphere than studio-bound dramas
Pierce Brosnan couldn't accept James Bond for GoldenEye initially because his Remington Steele contract was unexpectedly extended

Hart to Hart starred Robert Wagner and Stefanie Powers as a wealthy couple who stumble into mysteries

The Fall Guy starred Lee Majors as a Hollywood stuntman who moonlighted as a bounty hunter
The Fall Guy's theme 'The Unknown Stuntman' was performed by Lee Majors himself and charted on the country music charts
Scarecrow and Mrs. King starred Bruce Boxleitner and Kate Jackson as an unlikely spy duo in 1980s Washington D.C
Trapper John, M.D. was a sequel series set 28 years after M*A*S*H
St. Elsewhere was one of the first TV dramas to kill off a main character — Dr. White — midway through a season
St. Elsewhere, set in a run-down Boston hospital, became one of TV's most critically praised dramas of the 1980s
Hill Street Blues pioneered the serialized drama format on American television
Hill Street Blues won eight Emmy Awards in its first season in 1981, including Outstanding Drama Series
Hill Street Blues' morning roll call opening became a template copied by countless police procedurals in the decades that followed
Cagney & Lacey was the first US drama to star two women as equals in the lead roles
Cagney & Lacey was cancelled after its first season but fan letter campaigns convinced CBS to renew it
Murder, She Wrote ran for 12 seasons and made Angela Lansbury one of the highest-paid actors in television history

Angela Lansbury was initially reluctant to take the role of Jessica Fletcher
Bill Bixby, who played David Banner in The Incredible Hulk, also directed several episodes and pushed for more dramatic storylines
Lou Ferrigno, who played the Hulk, was genuinely deaf and worked with a sign language interpreter on set
The Incredible Hulk's melancholy closing theme became so linked to sad farewells that it was widely used in parody
The Six Million Dollar Man's bionic whir became one of the most recognized and parodied sound effects in TV history
The Bionic Woman spinoff was so popular it temporarily outrated the show it spun off
Lynda Carter performed many of her own stunts in Wonder Woman, including several involving the golden lasso
Wonder Woman's first season was set in World War II
21 Jump Street launched Johnny Depp's career
21 Jump Street was one of the first shows on the fledgling Fox network to become a genuine hit
Johnny Depp reportedly grew frustrated with his teen idol status from 21 Jump Street and actively sought edgier
The Love Boat was filmed almost entirely aboard actual Pacific Princess cruise ships
The Love Boat featured hundreds of guest stars across its nine seasons
Ricardo Montalbán's white suit in Fantasy Island became one of the most iconic TV costumes of the late 1970s
Hervé Villechaize, who played Tattoo on Fantasy Island, became iconic for his 'Ze plane! Ze plane!' catchphrase
WKRP in Cincinnati's Thanksgiving turkey-drop episode is consistently ranked among the greatest single episodes
The WKRP theme song's outro contained deliberately unintelligible lyrics
The M*A*S*H finale in 1983 drew 106 million viewers — a record for a series finale that stood for 27 years
M*A*S*H ran for 11 seasons, nearly four times longer than the actual Korean War it depicted
Barney Miller was filmed almost entirely on a single precinct set
Barney Miller was praised for portraying police officers as complex, overworked people rather than heroes, years before this became common
Three's Company was based on a British sitcom called Man About the House
John Ritter's physical comedy in Three's Company was so precise critics compared it favorably to classic silent film comedians like Keaton
The Golden Girls debuted in 1985 and consistently ranked in the top 10 for all seven of its seasons
All four main Golden Girls actresses won Emmy Awards for their roles
The Golden Girls was set in Miami specifically to justify the characters' warm-weather lifestyle and outdoor scenes
Bea Arthur, Betty White, Rue McClanahan, and Estelle Getty were all in their late 50s to 60s when Golden Girls debuted, defying TV's youth bias
Perfect Strangers debuted Bronson Pinchot's Balki Bartokomous and became one of the most beloved odd-couple comedies of the late 1980s
Perfect Strangers was set in Chicago and used real city locations for exterior shots across its eight-season run

Bob Newhart's deadpan telephone conversation style from The Bob Newhart Show carried over seamlessly into his Vermont innkeeper character
A Different World was a Cosby Show spinoff focusing on Denise Huxtable at a fictional historically Black college, running six seasons
Night Court was set in a real New York City night court and consultants helped the writers accurately depict
John Larroquette won four consecutive Emmy Awards for Supporting Actor for his role as Dan Fielding in Night Court
Designing Women was set in Atlanta and focused on a women-run interior design firm
L.A. Law ran from 1986-1994 and set the template for prestige ensemble workplace dramas in American television
L.A. Law won 15 Emmy Awards during its run and helped revive the legal drama genre in American prime-time television

thirtysomething was groundbreaking for featuring baby boomers grappling with middle-class anxieties rather than traditional TV drama

China Beach portrayed the Vietnam War from the perspective of military nurses and women
Northern Exposure (1990) used location shooting in Roslyn, Washington to portray the fictional Alaskan town of Cicely
In the Heat of the Night starred Carroll O'Connor as a Southern police chief and was praised for its nuanced
Spenser: For Hire was based on Robert B. Parker's popular detective novels and filmed on location in Boston

Highway to Heaven featured a different story each week with Landon and Victor French as an angel and his human partner helping others
Little House on the Prairie ended in 1983 with a finale where the town of Walnut Grove was literally dynamited to prevent a land grab
Mork & Mindy began as a Happy Days spinoff after Robin Williams' guest appearance as Mork became a surprise hit
Robin Williams improvised so often on Mork & Mindy that scripts had blank spaces marked 'Mork does stuff here'
The Fonz 'jumping the shark' on Happy Days gave rise to the phrase 'jumping the shark' for a show's creative decline after its peak
Henry Winkler, who played Fonzie, holds a master's degree from Yale School of Drama despite his iconic role
Laverne & Shirley was a Happy Days spinoff that at one point became the most watched show on American television
Penny Marshall, who played Laverne, later became one of the most successful female film directors in Hollywood
The Jeffersons ran for 11 seasons and was the longest-running primarily Black sitcom in American TV history
The Jeffersons was cancelled abruptly in 1985 with no finale, leaving the cast to learn of its cancellation through news reports
One Day at a Time was one of the first sitcoms to regularly feature a divorced single mother as the lead character
Taxi launched the careers of Andy Kaufman, Danny DeVito, and Christopher Lloyd simultaneously
Andy Kaufman's Latka Gravas character in Taxi was largely improvised and sometimes made the other actors break
SCTV launched the careers of John Candy, Martin Short, Catherine O'Hara, Rick Moranis, Eugene Levy, and Andrea Martin simultaneously
SCTV was originally produced in Canada on a shoestring budget
Saturday Night Live almost didn't survive the 1980s
Eddie Murphy joined SNL at 19 in 1980 and became the show's breakout star during a period of low ratings and cast turnover
DuckTales debuted in 1987 and became one of the highest-rated animated shows in the history of syndicated
DuckTales was based on Carl Barks' Uncle Scrooge comic books
The DuckTales theme song is one of the most recognized animated themes ever and was voted by fans as the best cartoon theme of all time
G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero premiered in 1983 and popularized the 'Knowing is half the battle' PSA segments
G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero ran from 1983-1986 and was produced by Sunbow Productions in partnership with Hasbro

The Transformers cartoon was produced partly in Japan by Toei Animation
Orson Welles voiced Unicron in the 1986 Transformers movie
He-Man and the Masters of the Universe debuted in 1983 as one of the first cartoons made primarily to sell a toy
At its peak, He-Man merchandise generated over $400 million in annual revenue
She-Ra: Princess of Power was created to give girls a He-Man equivalent and expand the Masters of the Universe toy franchise
ThunderCats was produced by Rankin/Bass and animated in Japan
Lion-O in ThunderCats is technically a child in an adult body
SilverHawks was created by the same team as ThunderCats and used a nearly identical production process
Voltron was adapted from two different Japanese anime series
Robotech was created by adapting three unrelated Japanese anime series
Robotech's serialized storytelling and mature themes were unusual for an American animated show in 1985
Inspector Gadget debuted in 1983 and was one of the first animated series to use computer assistance
Don Adams, who voiced Inspector Gadget, based the character's bumbling style on his Maxwell Smart character from Get Smart
The Smurfs became the highest-rated Saturday morning cartoon in the United States after its NBC debut in 1981
Smurfette was originally created by the villain Gargamel to cause chaos among the Smurfs
Scooby-Doo went through numerous format changes during the 1980s
Jim Henson created Fraggle Rock with a stated goal of ending conflict between nations
Fraggle Rock was produced simultaneously in multiple countries with different wraparound segments tailored to each nation's cultural context
The Muppet Show (1976-1981) was produced in the UK because no American network would pick it up as a primetime variety show
Pee-wee's Playhouse debuted in 1986 and won 22 Emmy Awards across its five seasons
Pee-wee's Playhouse featured a deliberately surreal aesthetic influenced by 1950s television and atomic-age design sensibilities
Captain Planet and the Planeteers (1990) was created with Ted Turner's explicit goal of teaching children environmental awareness
The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon debuted in 1987 as a five-part miniseries and became a full series

Each Ninja Turtle was named after a Renaissance artist — Leonardo, Donatello, Raphael, and Michelangelo

The Real Ghostbusters consistently altered the lore from the films

Jem featured completely original music for each episode
Danger Mouse was a British animated series that parodied spy fiction and became unexpectedly popular when aired
Double Dare debuted on Nickelodeon in 1986 and became the network's first original game show

The original 1978 Battlestar Galactica spawned a short-lived sequel series called Galactica 1980
Katee Sackhoff's female Starbuck in the reimagined BSG was initially controversial among fans but became one of the show's defining elements

KITT in Knight Rider was built on a 1982 Pontiac Trans Am; the red front scanner was inspired by the Cylons of Battlestar Galactica
The voice of KITT in Knight Rider was provided by actor William Daniels
Knight Rider's production team maintained a fleet of over a dozen Pontiac Trans Ams simultaneously
Knight Rider was created by Glen A. Larson, who also made Battlestar Galactica, Magnum P.I., and The Fall Guy
Knight Rider ran for four seasons from 1982 to 1986 and made David Hasselhoff an international superstar
Pontiac reported a significant sales increase in Trans Ams following Knight Rider's premiere
KITT's canopy in Knight Rider could not actually be opened from the inside during filming
Knight Rider spawned a 1991 TV movie, a 2000 follow-up, and a 2008 series — none matched the original's success
